Name: linguistic_priors_transfer
Title: Does Language Give a Free Lunch on Non-Linguistic Reasoning? Isolating the Transferable Compression Prior of Language Pretraining
Short Hypothesis: Pretraining on natural language endows models with a transferable, domain-general 'compression prior' (a bias toward hierarchical, compositional, recursively-structured representations) that improves learning of NON-linguistic structured tasks beyond what generic pretraining on structurally-matched but non-linguistic data provides. We hypothesize that language-pretrained models acquire abstract structural inductive biases that transfer to purely symbolic/perceptual reasoning problems, and that the transfer benefit scales with the compositional/hierarchical depth of the target task, revealing that part of AI 'intelligence' is a reusable structural prior imprinted by language rather than by language's content.
Related Work: Prior work shows language-model pretraining aids seemingly unrelated modalities: Lu et al. (2021, 'Frozen Pretrained Transformers') found LM-pretrained transformers transfer to numerical/vision tasks; Papadimitriou & Jurafsky (2020, 2023) showed non-linguistic and cross-domain pretraining (music, code, nested structure) transfers to language, isolating recursion/structure as the transferable ingredient. However, these establish that SOME structure transfers, mostly measuring the language-BENEFITS-from-X direction or coarse frozen-transformer performance. No work causally isolates WHICH property of language (its hierarchical/compositional structure vs its statistical n-gram surface vs its content) drives transfer TO non-linguistic reasoning, nor tests whether the transfer benefit scales specifically with target-task compositional depth via matched non-linguistic control pretraining corpora. We contribute a controlled 'structural-ablation of pretraining' design that dissociates language's abstract structure from its content and surface statistics, and maps the transfer benefit against a graded compositional-depth axis of downstream reasoning.
Abstract: Why does pretraining on natural language help models do things that have nothing to do with language? We ask whether language pretraining imparts a transferable, domain-general structural prior—a bias toward hierarchical, compositional, recursively-nested representations—that improves learning of purely non-linguistic reasoning tasks, and we try to isolate exactly which property of language causes it. We train small transformers (feasible in an academic lab: <=100M parameters) on a battery of matched pretraining corpora that ablate distinct properties of language: (1) natural language; (2) structure-preserving but content-free language (nested-bracket / dependency-tree-preserving nonce text that keeps hierarchical structure but destroys semantic content); (3) n-gram surface-matched but structure-destroyed text (shuffled to preserve local statistics but break hierarchy); (4) non-linguistic recursively-structured symbol streams (e.g., Dyck languages, arithmetic-expression trees); and (5) flat unstructured symbols. We then freeze most weights and probe transfer to a suite of NON-linguistic reasoning tasks graded by compositional depth: nested list manipulation, tree/graph traversal, symbolic algebra simplification, and multi-step arithmetic-expression evaluation. Our central prediction is a double dissociation: transfer to compositional tasks tracks the hierarchical-structure content of the pretraining corpus, not its surface statistics or semantic content, and the benefit grows with target-task compositional depth. We further test whether the transferable prior is localizable via representational-similarity and probing analyses. Results would identify a concrete, isolable mechanism—a compositional compression prior—by which language pretraining confers domain-general reasoning ability, sharpening the language–intelligence relationship into a testable structural claim.
Experiments: 1) PRETRAINING CORPORA (matched token budget, ~200M–500M tokens each): (a) NATURAL-LANGUAGE (English subset of a public corpus); (b) STRUCTURE-PRESERVING-NONCE—parse natural sentences, keep the dependency/constituency tree and function words but replace content words with nonce tokens (preserves hierarchy, destroys semantic content); (c) SURFACE-MATCHED-SHUFFLED—block-shuffle tokens to preserve n-gram statistics up to order k while destroying long-range hierarchy; (d) NON-LINGUISTIC-STRUCTURED—synthetic recursively-structured streams (Dyck-n bracket languages, nested arithmetic expression trees) with matched vocabulary size and token budget; (e) FLAT-CONTROL—i.i.d. random or Markov-1 symbol streams. All corpora use matched vocabulary size, sequence length, and token count. 2) MODELS: train identical small transformers (~30M and ~100M params) from scratch on each corpus to convergence (feasible on a single/few GPUs). 3) TRANSFER PROTOCOL: freeze all but input/output embeddings and a small readout head (frozen-pretrained-transformer style), then finetune on each downstream NON-linguistic reasoning task; also test full-finetuning and few-shot in-context settings. 4) DOWNSTREAM TASK SUITE graded by compositional depth: (i) nested list reversal/flattening, (ii) tree/graph traversal (find-ancestor, path length), (iii) symbolic algebra simplification, (iv) multi-step arithmetic-expression evaluation with parenthesization. Each task has a depth parameter (nesting depth / number of composition steps). 5) MAIN ANALYSES: (a) transfer accuracy and sample-efficiency (learning curves / area-under-curve) per pretraining corpus per task; (b) DOUBLE-DISSOCIATION test via mixed-effects regression: accuracy ~ pretrain_type * task_depth, predicting structured corpora (a,b,d) > surface/flat (c,e) and a positive structure*depth interaction; (c) does structure-preserving-nonce (b) match or approach natural language (a), isolating structure from content? (d) does non-linguistic-structured (d) recover most of the benefit, isolating structure from language per se? 6) MECHANISM: representational-similarity analysis (RSA/CKA) comparing hidden representations across pretraining types on shared probe inputs; train linear probes to decode nesting depth / bracket-matching state and test whether structured-pretrained models encode it more readily. 7) SCALING/GENERALIZATION: repeat at two model sizes and report scaling of the structure-transfer effect. METRICS: downstream accuracy, sample-efficiency (tokens/examples to threshold), structure*depth interaction coefficient and effect size, RSA/CKA similarity, probe decodability; all with seeds (>=3) and CIs via mixed-effects models (random effects for task and seed).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing structure-preserving-nonce and surface-matched-shuffled corpora that cleanly isolate hierarchy from statistics is delicate; residual leakage of structure or content is possible—mitigated by explicit n-gram statistic matching and parse-based nonce substitution, with corpus-level diagnostics reported. 2) Small-scale from-scratch models may show weaker or noisier transfer than large LLMs; we test two sizes and report scaling trends, treating small-scale isolation as the point (large opaque LLMs cannot be ablated cleanly). 3) Vocabulary/token-budget matching across such different corpora is imperfect; we hold vocabulary size and token count fixed and report these as covariates. 4) The 'compression prior' construct is operationalized via transfer + probing; alternative explanations (e.g., optimization landscape effects) are possible and discussed. 5) A null structure*depth interaction would still be informative, indicating language transfer is not primarily structural. 6) Downstream tasks are synthetic; ecological validity is limited, but synthetic control is necessary to grade compositional depth cleanly. 7) Freezing choices affect results; we report frozen, full-finetune, and in-context regimes to check robustness.
